name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: The Starbucks mermaid
items.fact: The two-tailed mermaid in the Starbucks logo was copied from an old Norse woodcut the founders found in a book. The first version, from 1971, was brown, not green.

items.name: Twitter's bird, Larry
items.fact: Twitter's blue bird logo had a name: Larry, after the basketball player Larry Bird of the Boston Celtics. One of Twitter's founders, Biz Stone, comes from Boston.

items.name: The FedEx arrow
items.fact: The FedEx logo hides a white arrow in the space between the “E” and the “x”. Its designer, Lindon Leader, wanted it to suggest speed, but many people never notice it.

items.name: The bite in Apple's apple
items.fact: Designer Rob Janoff added the bite to Apple's logo in 1977 so that, at small sizes, people would see an apple and not a cherry.

items.name: Toblerone's hidden bear
items.fact: The mountain on the Toblerone logo hides the shape of a bear, the symbol of Bern, the Swiss city where the chocolate was first made.

items.name: Chupa Chups and Salvador Dalí
items.fact: The daisy-shaped logo of the Spanish lollipop brand Chupa Chups was designed in 1969 by the surrealist painter Salvador Dalí. He reportedly sketched it in under an hour.

items.name: Baskin-Robbins' hidden 31
items.fact: The pink parts of the “BR” in the Baskin-Robbins logo form the number 31, for the ice-cream chain's famous 31 flavours: one for every day of the month.

items.name: I ♥ NY
items.fact: Milton Glaser sketched the “I ♥ NY” logo in red crayon in the back of a New York taxi in 1977. He did the job for free, and it became one of the world's most copied logos.

items.name: Gap's one-week logo
items.fact: In 2010 the clothing brand Gap replaced its classic blue-box logo with a new design. Customers hated it so much online that Gap went back to the old one after about a week.

items.name: Coca-Cola's handwriting
items.fact: The flowing Coca-Cola logo wasn't made by a designer. In the 1880s it was written by Frank Mason Robinson, the bookkeeper of the drink's inventor, in a handwriting style popular at the time.

fakes.name: The upside-down swallow
fakes.fact: A Portuguese sardine brand, Marés do Norte, printed its swallow logo upside down by mistake in 1952. Sales went up, so the bird has flown upside down ever since.

fakes.name: A fox drawn by a child
fakes.fact: The fox in the logo of a Finnish outdoor-clothing brand, Kettuvaara, was drawn by the founder's nine-year-old daughter in 1974. She still gets a free jacket every winter.

fakes.name: A logo chosen by cows
fakes.fact: A Dutch cheese brand chose its logo by putting three designs on boards in a field and picking the one its cows stood next to most often.

fakes.name: A font from a gravestone
fakes.fact: The lettering of a British tea brand, Hartley & Moss, was copied from the gravestone of the founder's grandfather in a Yorkshire churchyard.

fakes.name: The coastline wave
fakes.fact: The wave in the logo of a Norwegian ferry company, Havbris, is the exact outline of the coast between Bergen and Ålesund, traced from an old sea map.

fakes.name: The bus driver's logo
fakes.fact: An Italian pasta maker let radio listeners choose its new logo in 1965. The winning design came from a bus driver in Naples, who was paid in pasta for a year.

fakes.name: The coffee-stain logo
fakes.fact: The brown ring in the logo of a Swedish café chain, Brunbönan, is a real coffee stain, scanned from a page of the founder's notebook in 1993.

fakes.name: The green of a sweater
fakes.fact: A German running-shoe brand, Sprintwald, copied its exact shade of green from the sweater the founder's wife wore on the day the company was registered.

fakes.name: The upside-down bike logo
fakes.fact: A Japanese bicycle brand, Hayate Cycles, made its logo read the same upside down, so it looks right whether a bike is standing in a shop or hanging from the ceiling.

fakes.name: The hidden mouse
fakes.fact: The logo of a Belgian chocolate maker has a tiny mouse hidden inside the letter “o”, added by the designer as a joke. The company only noticed twenty years later.
